sm: Host Keith Foskey opens a special episode of the Your Calvinist podcast about Calvary Chapel Costa Mesa. A video showed its pastor, Chaz Broderson, defending the ordination of women. He argued that Paul's ban on women teaching and holding authority over men was a response to the cult of Artemis in Ephesus, not a universal rule. That is an egalitarian view, in contrast to the movement's historic complementarian position. Keith's guest is his friend David Guzik, author of the Enduring Word Bible commentary. David describes himself as a lifelong Calvary Chapel man who was converted at Calvary Chapel Riverside under Greg Laurie. He has pastored three Calvary Chapel churches, directed a Bible college campus in Germany for seven years, and now attends Calvary Chapel Santa Barbara.

Keith asks David to define complementarianism and egalitarianism. David says complementarians hold that men and women are equal in worth and salvation, but that God assigned leadership of the home to the husband and leadership of the church to qualified men. He stresses the word qualified, since the Bible lists specific requirements. Egalitarians, he says, see no distinction in roles between men and women. Keith adds that he believes in male leadership and does not see patriarchy as a separate camp. David says Chuck Smith, the founder, was firmly complementarian, and that he reportedly did not even want women greeters. The one known exception was Corrie ten Boom speaking once, and there were never women pastors, elders or board members.

The two note that women like Corrie ten Boom and Joni Eareckson Tada spoke at special occasions without changing church order. Keith asks whether Chaz Broderson, Chuck Smith's grandson, is changing course. David says Broderson said in two messages, on November 1st and 8th, that the practice has been in place about ten years without being announced, even though earlier denials were made under his father Brian. Broderson presented it as the congregation's position. Keith says he is about to speak at a conference on hell, ecclesiology, and women pastors. He then summarizes Broderson's argument that the teaching women were influenced by Artemis priestesses and that the Greek word for authority means to wrestle for authority.

David finds Broderson's case very unpersuasive and says egalitarian arguments on this passage are often contradictory. If false women teachers were the problem, he asks, why would Paul silence all women rather than silence false teachers of both sexes? He also notes that the ban only covers teaching men, which would leave women teaching women acceptable. He doubts that Ephesus was a unique case in an otherwise egalitarian early church. Keith points out that Paul grounds his instruction in creation, not local circumstances, and David agrees the reasons are universal. Both say the Artemis reading is a recent novelty absent from centuries of commentary.

Keith notes that Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy also hold to male leadership, and David calls the idea of a gender-neutral earliest church a historical fantasy. Keith argues that First Timothy 2:12 forbids women the two things pastors must do, teach and exercise authority, and that elders must be apt to teach. He says people who support women pastors usually take one of two routes. One is to say Paul was wrong or sexist, which Keith associates with liberal churches. The other is to find an exegetical loophole, such as limiting the text to Ephesus. David adds a third, using Galatians 3:28 to override the passage, which he calls a wrong hermeneutic since Scripture should be harmonized.

David says it is rare to find an egalitarian who affirms the husband's headship at home but denies male church leadership, since the two principles tend to stand or fall together. Keith shares that at his daughter's wedding he used the traditional vows, including the word obey, which surprised the groom's father. They then turn to First Corinthians 14, where women are told to be silent. David does not recall the textual issues but says the context is the judging of prophecy, which belongs to qualified male leaders. Keith agrees that the principle is not limited to Corinth.

Keith asks what happens to the qualifications for elders and deacons in First Timothy 3 if the whole letter is only about Ephesus. David says that logic has no stopping point, since the line between local and universal becomes arbitrary. Both note that the qualifications, such as husband of one wife and ruling one's household well, have a masculine character. Keith adds that the twelve apostles were all men. They reject the argument that Junia was a woman apostle greater than Paul, noting she is named alongside Andronicus. David says Jesus could easily have chosen women among the twelve, and that women's service is honored in Scripture without anyone holding congregational office. Keith then raises claims about Phoebe being the interpreter of Romans.

David says he has found no ancient evidence that the carrier of a letter was regarded as its authoritative interpreter, so the Phoebe claim is a fantasy. He has seen ten or twelve theories used to set aside First Timothy 2, and calls the Artemis argument another grasp for a reason to avoid the plain sense. They say they are not questioning Broderson's integrity, only his interpretive method. David says someone can be wrong on this and still be a brother or sister in Christ, but the error has significant consequences for how churches function. Closing, he says Costa Mesa is an outlier today, and that overwhelmingly Calvary Chapel pastors hold the biblical roles of men and women in church and home.
